claim: The fusion of mammalian gametes requires the interaction between IZUMO1 on the sperm and JUNO on the oocyte.
source: The fusion of mammalian gametes requires the interaction between IZUMO1 on the sperm and JUNO on the oocyte.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript to prior work establishing this interaction.

claim: Ectopic expression of mouse IZUMO1 induces cell-cell fusion.
source: We have recently shown that ectopic expression of mouse IZUMO1 induces cell-cell fusion and that sperm can fuse to fibroblasts expressing JUNO.
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Brukman et al., 2023) as indicated by the citation context.

claim: Sperm can fuse to fibroblasts expressing JUNO.
source: We have recently shown that ectopic expression of mouse IZUMO1 induces cell-cell fusion and that sperm can fuse to fibroblasts expressing JUNO.
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Brukman et al., 2023).

claim: Incubation of mouse sperm with hamster fibroblasts or human epithelial cells in culture induces the fusion between these somatic cells and the formation of syncytia.
source: Here, we found that the incubation of mouse sperm with hamster fibroblasts or human epithelial cells in culture induces the fusion between these somatic cells and the formation of syncytia, a pattern previously observed with some animal viruses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-5.

claim: Sperm-induced cell-cell fusion requires a species-matching JUNO on both fusing cells.
source: This sperm-induced cell-cell fusion requires a species-matching JUNO on both fusing cells, can be blocked by an antibody against IZUMO1, and does not rely on the synthesis of new proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that both cell populations need JUNO for fusion, and Figure 4 showing species-specificity.

claim: Sperm-induced cell-cell fusion can be blocked by an antibody against IZUMO1.
source: This sperm-induced cell-cell fusion requires a species-matching JUNO on both fusing cells, can be blocked by an antibody against IZUMO1, and does not rely on the synthesis of new proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B showing that anti-IZUMO1 antibody blocks both sperm-BHK fusion and multinucleation.

claim: Sperm-induced cell-cell fusion does not rely on the synthesis of new proteins.
source: This sperm-induced cell-cell fusion requires a species-matching JUNO on both fusing cells, can be blocked by an antibody against IZUMO1, and does not rely on the synthesis of new proteins.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and D showing that cycloheximide treatment does not affect multinucleation levels.

claim: The fusion is dependent on the sperm's fusogenic capacity.
source: The fusion is dependent on the sperm's fusogenic capacity, making this a reliable, fast, and simple method for predicting sperm function during the diagnosis of male infertility.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing that non-capacitated sperm fail to induce fusion, and correlation data in Figure 3C-D showing relationship with fertilization ability.

claim: Infertility is estimated to affect approximately 15% of the population.
source: Infertility is estimated to affect approximately 15% of the population (World Health Organization, 2023), and many couples dealing with this burden turn to assisted reproductive techniques (ARTs) as a possible solution (Steptoe and Edwards, 1978; Palermo et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization, 2023.

claim: The hamster oocyte penetration (HOP) test has been proposed as a quantitative method for analyzing the fusogenic potential of human spermatozoa.
source: The hamster oocyte penetration (HOP) test has been proposed as a quantitative method for analyzing the fusogenic potential of human spermatozoa (Aitken and Elton, 1986; Yanagimachi et al., 1976; Zainul Rashid et al., 1998), however, it was excluded from the newest WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen (World Health Organization HRP, 2021) for being considered obsolete.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aitken and Elton, 1986; Yanagimachi et al., 1976; Zainul Rashid et al., 1998.

claim: The HOP test was excluded from the newest WHO laboratory manual for being considered obsolete.
source: The hamster oocyte penetration (HOP) test has been proposed as a quantitative method for analyzing the fusogenic potential of human spermatozoa (Aitken and Elton, 1986; Yanagimachi et al., 1976; Zainul Rashid et al., 1998), however, it was excluded from the newest WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen (World Health Organization HRP, 2021) for being considered obsolete.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to World Health Organization HRP, 2021.

claim: There is no standardized methodology to analyze specifically the ability of sperm to fuse to oocytes.
source: Therefore, to date, there is no other standardized methodology to analyze specifically the ability of sperm to fuse to oocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion following the discussion of the HOP test being obsolete.

claim: In mammals, the adhesion of the sperm to the oocyte plasma membranes is mediated by the species-specific interaction of IZUMO1 and JUNO.
source: In mammals, the adhesion of the sperm to the oocyte plasma membranes is mediated by the species-specific interaction of two membrane proteins: IZUMO1 and JUNO (Bianchi and Wright, 2015; Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016; Matsumura et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Bianchi and Wright, 2015; Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016; Matsumura et al., 2021.

claim: IZUMO1 is expressed during spermatogenesis and localizes to the fusogenic region of the sperm head after acrosome reaction.
source: The transmembrane protein IZUMO1 is expressed during spermatogenesis and localizes to the fusogenic region of the sperm head after an exocytic process named acrosome reaction (Inoue et al., 2005; Satouh et al., 2012; Inoue et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Inoue et al., 2005; Satouh et al., 2012; Inoue et al., 2015; Nishimura et al., 2016.

claim: JUNO is an oocyte protein bound to the plasma membrane by a GPI lipid anchor.
source: On the other hand, the IZUMO1 receptor, JUNO, is an oocyte protein bound to the plasma membrane by a GPI lipid anchor (Bianchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bianchi et al., 2014.

claim: The fusion of the two gametes relies on the action of IZUMO1 in a unilateral manner.
source: The subsequent fusion of the two gametes relies on the action of IZUMO1 in a unilateral manner (Brukman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brukman et al., 2023.

claim: The IZUMO1-JUNO interaction was characterized in humans.
source: The IZUMO1-JUNO interaction was characterized also in humans (Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016) and its relevance for human fertility is supported by the presence of antibodies against IZUMO1 in the sera of immuno-infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), the mutations on JUNO in cases of fertilization failure and polyspermy (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), and the lower levels of IZUMO1 observed in sperm that failed to fertilize during in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016.

claim: Antibodies against IZUMO1 are present in the sera of immuno-infertile women.
source: The IZUMO1-JUNO interaction was characterized also in humans (Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016) and its relevance for human fertility is supported by the presence of antibodies against IZUMO1 in the sera of immuno-infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), the mutations on JUNO in cases of fertilization failure and polyspermy (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), and the lower levels of IZUMO1 observed in sperm that failed to fertilize during in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022.

claim: Mutations on JUNO occur in cases of fertilization failure and polyspermy.
source: The IZUMO1-JUNO interaction was characterized also in humans (Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016) and its relevance for human fertility is supported by the presence of antibodies against IZUMO1 in the sera of immuno-infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), the mutations on JUNO in cases of fertilization failure and polyspermy (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), and the lower levels of IZUMO1 observed in sperm that failed to fertilize during in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022.

claim: Lower levels of IZUMO1 are observed in sperm that failed to fertilize during in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments.
source: The IZUMO1-JUNO interaction was characterized also in humans (Aydin et al., 2016; Ohto et al., 2016) and its relevance for human fertility is supported by the presence of antibodies against IZUMO1 in the sera of immuno-infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), the mutations on JUNO in cases of fertilization failure and polyspermy (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022), and the lower levels of IZUMO1 observed in sperm that failed to fertilize during in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments (Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clark and Naz, 2013; Yu et al., 2018; Enoiu et al., 2022.

claim: Mouse sperm can fuse to fibroblasts ectopically expressing JUNO.
source: Recently, we found that mouse sperm can fuse to fibroblasts ectopically expressing the sperm-receptor JUNO (Brukman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Brukman et al., 2023).

claim: After sperm fuses with a somatic cell, this cell can fuse with additional cells inducing syncytia formation.
source: Here, we show that after sperm fuses with a somatic cell, this cell can fuse with additional cells inducing syncytia formation - a single cell with several nuclei (multinucleated cell).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Sperm-induced cell-cell fusion is possibly mediated by the bridging of a single sperm simultaneously fused to two different cells.
source: This is possibly mediated by the bridging of a single sperm simultaneously fused to two different cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing that temporally uncoupling sperm-BHK and BHK-BHK fusion does not result in content mixing.

claim: Sperm with higher fertilizing ability can induce the fusion of somatic cells more efficiently.
source: We found that sperm with higher fertilizing ability can induce the fusion of somatic cells more efficiently, judged by the increased levels of multinucleation.
evidence: This is supported by correlation data in Figure 3C-D showing positive correlation between multinucleation and fertilization rates.

claim: Mouse sperm cells only fuse to Baby Hamster Kidney (BHK) cells if they are induced to express JUNO.
source: In our experimental conditions, mouse sperm cells only fuse to Baby Hamster Kidney (BHK) cells if they are induced to express the sperm-receptor, JUNO (Brukman et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and references prior work (Brukman et al., 2023).

claim: Sperm induces the formation of multinucleated BHK cells (syncytia).
source: Surprisingly, we found that sperm induces the formation of multinucleated BHK cells (syncytia; Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The induction of multinucleation was dependent on the presence of JUNO.
source: The induction of multinucleation was dependent on the presence of JUNO (Figure 1B–C), however, JUNO expression alone is not sufficient to induce this process.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1B-C showing no multinucleation in cells without JUNO.

claim: JUNO expression alone is not sufficient to induce multinucleation.
source: The induction of multinucleation was dependent on the presence of JUNO (Figure 1B–C), however, JUNO expression alone is not sufficient to induce this process.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C showing that only JUNO-expressing cells with fused sperm form syncytia.

claim: Only cells with sperm fused to them form syncytia.
source: Only cells with sperm fused to them form syncytia (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C distinguishing multinucleation in JUNO cells with and without fused sperm.

claim: Bigger syncytia tend to contain more sperm.
source: Furthermore, bigger syncytia tend to contain more sperm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and the levels of multinucleation were dependent on the amount of sperm added to the cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing distribution of sperm numbers in cells with different numbers of nuclei.

claim: The levels of multinucleation were dependent on the amount of sperm added to the cells.
source: Furthermore, bigger syncytia tend to contain more sperm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and the levels of multinucleation were dependent on the amount of sperm added to the cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing increased multinucleation with more sperm.

claim: The fusion of sperm with JUNO-expressing BHK cells is required for inducing subsequent multinucleation of these somatic cells.
source: Thus, the fusion of sperm with JUNO-expressing BHK cells is required for inducing subsequent multinucleation of these somatic cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 1 showing JUNO and sperm fusion are both required.

claim: Some somatic cells can fuse following viral infection.
source: However, decades ago, it was first described that some somatic cells can fuse following viral infection (Okada, 1962; Kohn, 1965) and later confirmed for diverse viruses, including SARS-CoV2 (Buchrieser et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Okada, 1962; Kohn, 1965; Buchrieser et al., 2020.

claim: Some viruses induce Fusion From Within (FFWI) which requires the synthesis of new viral proteins.
source: This process may require the synthesis of new viral proteins and, therefore, induces Fusion From Within (FFWI) while other viruses induce fusion independently of protein synthesis in a process called Fusion From Without (FFWO) (Bratt and Gallaher, 1969; Duelli and Lazebnik, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bratt and Gallaher, 1969; Duelli and Lazebnik, 2007.

claim: Some viruses induce Fusion From Without (FFWO) which is independent of protein synthesis.
source: This process may require the synthesis of new viral proteins and, therefore, induces Fusion From Within (FFWI) while other viruses induce fusion independently of protein synthesis in a process called Fusion From Without (FFWO) (Bratt and Gallaher, 1969; Duelli and Lazebnik, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bratt and Gallaher, 1969; Duelli and Lazebnik, 2007.

claim: Orthoreoviruses induce the expression of fusion-associated small transmembrane (FAST) proteins upon infection, promoting FFWI.
source: For instance, orthoreoviruses induce the expression of fusion-associated small transmembrane (FAST) proteins upon infection, promoting FFWI (Ciechonska et al., 2014; Theuerkauf et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ciechonska et al., 2014; Theuerkauf et al., 2021.

claim: De novo protein synthesis is not required for the induction of multinucleation by sperm.
source: We found no differences in the levels of multinucleation between control and cycloheximide treatments (Figure 1B and D). This shows that de novo protein synthesis is not required for the induction of multinucleation by sperm and suggests a mechanism of FFWO.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and D showing cycloheximide does not affect multinucleation.

claim: Sperm use a mechanism of Fusion From Without (FFWO) when fibroblasts express JUNO.
source: This shows that de novo protein synthesis is not required for the induction of multinucleation by sperm and suggests a mechanism of FFWO.
evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide experiment showing protein synthesis is not required.

claim: Fusion between cells occurs efficiently within 10–15 min after the addition of the sperm.
source: Additionally, live imaging of the process showed that fusion between cells occurs efficiently within 10–15 min after the addition of the sperm (Figure 1E, Video 1), suggesting that protein synthesis is not involved.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: Sperm use a viral-like mechanism of FFWO when the fibroblasts express the oocyte JUNO in vitro.
source: Even though it is not known whether sperm can induce the fusion of somatic cells in vivo, we show that sperm use a viral-like mechanism of FFWO when the fibroblasts express the oocyte JUNO in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cycloheximide and time-lapse experiments.

claim: Sperm-induced multinucleation is a consequence of BHK-BHK cell fusion.
source: Then we asked whether the sperm-induced multinucleation was a consequence of BHK-BHK cell fusion and if so, whether it requires JUNO to be present on both fusing cells.
evidence: This is confirmed by content-mixing experiments in Figure 2 showing formation of hybrid cells with both fluorescent markers.

claim: Multinucleated hybrid cells containing both fluorescent markers were observed, confirming the fusion of BHK cells expressing JUNO.
source: We observed the formation of multinucleated hybrid cells containing both fluorescent markers, confirming the fusion of BHK cells expressing JUNO (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by content-mixing data in Figure 2 showing cells with both green and red markers.

claim: BHK-BHK cell fusion was not observed when only one or neither of the cell populations expressed JUNO.
source: This BHK-BHK cell fusion was not observed when only one or neither of the cell populations expressed JUNO (Figure 2B–C), indicating that sperm-induced multinucleation is indeed BHK-BHK cell fusion which relies on bilateral expression of JUNO.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B-C showing no content mixing without bilateral JUNO expression.

claim: Sperm-induced multinucleation relies on bilateral expression of JUNO.
source: This BHK-BHK cell fusion was not observed when only one or neither of the cell populations expressed JUNO (Figure 2B–C), indicating that sperm-induced multinucleation is indeed BHK-BHK cell fusion which relies on bilateral expression of JUNO.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the content-mixing experiments in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of an inhibitor of the cell cycle (FdUdr) does not inhibit multinucleation.
source: However, the presence of an inhibitor of the cell cycle (FdUdr, 5-fluoro-2′-deoxyuridine, Valansi et al., 2017) does not inhibit multinucleation (Figure 3A–B), ruling out that syncytia formation is as a consequence of failure in the division of the BHK cells and confirming the occurrence of fusion between them.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B showing FdUdr does not reduce multinucleation.

claim: Syncytia formation is not a consequence of failure in the division of the BHK cells.
source: However, the presence of an inhibitor of the cell cycle (FdUdr, 5-fluoro-2′-deoxyuridine, Valansi et al., 2017) does not inhibit multinucleation (Figure 3A–B), ruling out that syncytia formation is as a consequence of failure in the division of the BHK cells and confirming the occurrence of fusion between them.
evidence: This is inferred from the FdUdr experiment showing cell cycle inhibition does not prevent multinucleation.

claim: IZUMO1 fades from the sperm after fusion to the fibroblast.
source: We have previously shown that IZUMO1 fades from the sperm after fusion to the fibroblast (Brukman et al., 2023) indicating that this transmembrane protein is transferred to the target cell plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Brukman et al., 2023).

claim: IZUMO1 is transferred to the target cell plasma membrane after sperm fusion.
source: We have previously shown that IZUMO1 fades from the sperm after fusion to the fibroblast (Brukman et al., 2023) indicating that this transmembrane protein is transferred to the target cell plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IZUMO1 fades from sperm and is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: IZUMO1 was observed diffusing to the oocyte plasma membrane during in vitro fertilization assays.
source: Consistent with these findings, IZUMO1 was observed diffusing to the oocyte plasma membrane during in vitro fertilization assays (Satouh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Satouh et al., 2012.

claim: IZUMO1 diffuses from the sperm head after its fusion with the BHK cell.
source: Here, we detected IZUMO1 by immunostaining and by a fluorescent reporter and confirmed that it diffuses from the sperm head after its fusion with the BHK cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B), suggesting a function for the fusogenic machinery carried by the sperm during the FFWO process.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and fluorescent reporter data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: When sperm were first allowed to fuse with one population of green cells before adding the second population of red cells, hybrid syncytia were not observed.
source: However, when sperm were first allowed to fuse with one population of green cells before adding the second population of red cells, hybrid syncytia were not observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B showing no content mixing in the two-step assay.

claim: It is not possible to uncouple temporarily the sperm-BHK and BHK-BHK cell fusions.
source: These results suggest that it is not possible to uncouple temporarily the sperm-BHK and BHK-BHK cell fusions, arguing against the model of transfer of fusion proteins and suggesting that sperm are fusing simultaneously to two cells using a sperm sandwich mechanism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Cii).
evidence: This is inferred from the two-step fusion experiment results in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sperm are fusing simultaneously to two cells using a sperm sandwich mechanism.
source: These results suggest that it is not possible to uncouple temporarily the sperm-BHK and BHK-BHK cell fusions, arguing against the model of transfer of fusion proteins and suggesting that sperm are fusing simultaneously to two cells using a sperm sandwich mechanism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2Cii).
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to temporally separate sperm-BHK and BHK-BHK fusion events.

claim: Sperm cells incubated in media lacking BSA or Ca2+ failed to fuse to BHK cells.
source: We found that sperm cells incubated under these conditions failed to fuse to BHK cells, as well as to induce syncytia formation (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B showing no fusion or multinucleation without BSA or Ca2+.

claim: Sperm cells incubated in media lacking BSA or Ca2+ failed to induce syncytia formation.
source: We found that sperm cells incubated under these conditions failed to fuse to BHK cells, as well as to induce syncytia formation (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: BHK-BHK cell fusion requires fully capacitated sperm.
source: Thus, BHK-BHK cell fusion requires fully capacitated sperm.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments showing non-capacitated sperm fail to induce fusion.

claim: A positive and significant correlation exists between syncytia formation and the levels of fertilization.
source: We detected a positive and significant correlation between the syncytia formation and the levels of fertilization, evaluated with complete and denuded oocytes (Figure 3C–D, Source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis in Figure 3C-D showing Pearson's r values and p<0.05.

claim: BHK multinucleation did not correlate with the percentage of acrosome reaction of capacitated sperm.
source: In contrast, BHK multinucleation did not correlate with the percentage of acrosome reaction of capacitated sperm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that SPICER relies not only on capacitation but on the overall sperm fertilizing potential.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing no significant correlation.

claim: SPICER relies not only on capacitation but on the overall sperm fertilizing potential.
source: In contrast, BHK multinucleation did not correlate with the percentage of acrosome reaction of capacitated sperm (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that SPICER relies not only on capacitation but on the overall sperm fertilizing potential.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation with acrosome reaction but positive correlation with fertilization.

claim: IZUMO1 is essential for sperm-egg interactions via binding to JUNO.
source: The sperm IZUMO1 protein is essential for sperm-egg interactions via binding to JUNO (Bianchi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bianchi et al., 2014.

claim: IZUMO1 was shown to induce the fusion of cells in a JUNO-independent way using a different domain.
source: More recently, IZUMO1 was shown to induce the fusion of cells in a JUNO-independent way using a different domain that is not required for binding to the egg receptor (Brukman et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brukman et al., 2023.

claim: The anti-IZUMO1 antibody had the ability to block both sperm-BHK and sperm-induced BHK-BHK cell fusions.
source: We found that the anti-IZUMO1 antibody had the ability to block both sperm-BHK and sperm-induced BHK-BHK cell fusions even when sperm cells were fully capacitated (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B showing blocking with anti-IZUMO1 antibody.

claim: The SPICER assay is able to determine sperm fertilization potential that depends on the IZUMO1-JUNO interactions.
source: Altogether, our results show that the SPICER assay is able to determine sperm fertilization potential that depends on the IZUMO1-JUNO interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody blocking and correlation experiments.

claim: IZUMO1-JUNO interactions show species-specific selectivity among different mammalian species.
source: Elegant work on IZUMO1-JUNO interactions among different mammalian species has shown species-specific selectivity between these crucial interactions (Bianchi and Wright, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bianchi and Wright, 2015.

claim: Lower levels of sperm-BHK cell fusion were observed with human JUNO compared to mouse JUNO.
source: Under these conditions, we observed lower levels of sperm-BHK cell fusion and a reduction in BHK cell multinucleation compared to cells expressing mouse JUNO (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-C comparing mouse and human JUNO.

claim: A reduction in BHK cell multinucleation was observed with human JUNO compared to mouse JUNO.
source: Under these conditions, we observed lower levels of sperm-BHK cell fusion and a reduction in BHK cell multinucleation compared to cells expressing mouse JUNO (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The low activity mediated by human JUNO was still significant compared to the control without JUNO.
source: Interestingly, the low activity mediated by human JUNO was still significant compared to the control without JUNO.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis in Figure 4 showing significant differences from control.

claim: There is a residual cross-interaction between mouse sperm and human JUNO.
source: This confirms the requirement of a species-matching JUNO for the assay; however, it puts in evidence a residual cross-interaction between mouse sperm and human JUNO.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that human JUNO shows reduced but still significant activity with mouse sperm.

claim: When hamster JUNO was employed, no differences were observed compared to mouse JUNO.
source: On the contrary, when hamster JUNO was employed, no differences were observed compared to mouse JUNO (Figure 4A–C), consistent with the promiscuous nature of the hamster oocytes (Bianchi and Wright, 2015; Nakajima et al., 2022; Hanada and Chang, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-C and citations to prior work.

claim: Hamster oocytes have a promiscuous nature.
source: On the contrary, when hamster JUNO was employed, no differences were observed compared to mouse JUNO (Figure 4A–C), consistent with the promiscuous nature of the hamster oocytes (Bianchi and Wright, 2015; Nakajima et al., 2022; Hanada and Chang, 1972).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bianchi and Wright, 2015; Nakajima et al., 2022; Hanada and Chang, 1972.

claim: HEK cells bearing JUNO fused between them when they were co-incubated with sperm.
source: As observed for the BHK cells, HEK cells bearing JUNO fused between them when they were co-incubated with sperm (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-C using the Dual Split Protein system.

claim: HEK cells without JUNO did not show content mixing.
source: On the contrary, neither HEK cells without JUNO nor HEK expressing JUNO but without sperm showed content mixing (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-C showing no GFP assembly without JUNO or sperm.

claim: HEK cells expressing JUNO but without sperm did not show content mixing.
source: On the contrary, neither HEK cells without JUNO nor HEK expressing JUNO but without sperm showed content mixing (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The fusion was dependent on the co-incubation time reaching a maximum at around 4 hr.
source: The fusion was dependent on the co-incubation time reaching a maximum at around 4 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-course data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SPICER is not restricted to BHK cells or fibroblasts.
source: These results show that SPICER is not restricted to BHK cells or fibroblasts and opens the possibility of adapting this assay to different cell lines and approaches to evaluate cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful demonstration of SPICER in HEK cells in addition to BHK cells.

claim: JUNO has been described in lymphoid tissues.
source: Apart from being expressed in oocytes, JUNO has been described in lymphoid tissues (Spiegelstein et al., 2000), more specifically in regulatory T cells (Yamaguchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spiegelstein et al., 2000 and Yamaguchi et al., 2007.

claim: JUNO is expressed in regulatory T cells.
source: Apart from being expressed in oocytes, JUNO has been described in lymphoid tissues (Spiegelstein et al., 2000), more specifically in regulatory T cells (Yamaguchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2007.

claim: Sperm fusion to somatic cells cannot occur before acrosomal exocytosis, when IZUMO1 is enclosed into the acrosome.
source: This fusion cannot occur before acrosomal exocytosis, when IZUMO1 is enclosed into the acrosome (Inoue et al., 2005; Satouh et al., 2012), and therefore, it will be relevant to study sperm fusion to somatic cells within the oviduct of the female, close to the fertilization site (Muro et al., 2016; Hino et al., 2016; La Spina et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Inoue et al., 2005; Satouh et al., 2012.

claim: JUNO was detected in the first polar body.
source: Furthermore, JUNO was detected in the first polar body (Suzuki et al., 2017) and whether sperm can fuse to it or if sperm fusion to the oocyte can induce the polar body-egg fusion remains unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2017.

claim: IZUMO1-JUNO interaction is a specific requirement during sperm-egg fusion of mammals.
source: Furthermore, even though IZUMO1-JUNO interaction is a specific requirement during sperm-egg fusion of mammals (Grayson, 2015), we cannot exclude that alternative configurations, using the right egg receptors (Lu and Ikawa, 2022), will be possible in the future to induce somatic cell-cell fusion by sperm of other sexually reproducing organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grayson, 2015.

claim: In species where Izumo1 and Izumo1r genes are absent, such as plants and protists, the gamete fusion is promoted by the fusogen HAPLESS 2/GENERATIVE CELL-SPECIFIC 1 (HAP2/GCS1).
source: In species where Izumo1 and Izumo1r genes are absent, such as plants and protists, the gamete fusion is promoted by the fusogen HAPLESS 2/GENERATIVE CELL-SPECIFIC 1 (HAP2/GCS1) (Brukman et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brukman et al., 2021.

claim: IZUMO1 orthologs were described in zebrafish and nematodes.
source: In other organisms like zebrafish or nematodes, IZUMO1 orthologs were described (Binner et al., 2021; Nishimura et al., 2015; Takayama et al., 2021) but, since JUNO is present only in mammals (Vance and Lee, 2020; Grayson, 2015), it is unclear whether male gametes in other species interact with different receptors on the female gamete.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Binner et al., 2021; Nishimura et al., 2015; Takayama et al., 2021.

claim: JUNO is present only in mammals.
source: In other organisms like zebrafish or nematodes, IZUMO1 orthologs were described (Binner et al., 2021; Nishimura et al., 2015; Takayama et al., 2021) but, since JUNO is present only in mammals (Vance and Lee, 2020; Grayson, 2015), it is unclear whether male gametes in other species interact with different receptors on the female gamete.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vance and Lee, 2020; Grayson, 2015.

claim: The HOP assay became obsolete.
source: Considering that the HOP assay became obsolete, an assay that evaluates the fusion of somatic cells with ectopic expression of JUNO induced by competent sperm (SPICER, Figure 6) represents a powerful diagnostic tool.
evidence: This is stated based on the WHO manual exclusion mentioned earlier in the manuscript.

claim: SPICER could potentially predict the success chances of ARTs like intrauterine insemination (IUI) or conventional IVF.
source: SPICER could potentially predict the success chances of ARTs like intrauterine insemination (IUI) or conventional IVF, which require a fusion-competent sperm, and if it is necessary to proceed with a more complex technique such as intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of SPICER.

claim: ICSI is associated with a slightly higher risk of adverse outcomes in the progeny.
source: This is particularly important considering the routine use of the ICSI is under debate as it is associated with a slightly higher risk of adverse outcomes in the progeny (Practice Committees of the American Society for Practice Committees of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Practice Committees of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology, 2020.

claim: Significantly lower levels of IZUMO1 were detected in the sperm cells of patients with total fertilization failure.
source: Considering our previous work showing that IZUMO1 can mediate cell-cell fusion (Brukman et al., 2023) and that significantly lower levels of this protein were detected in the sperm cells of patients with total fertilization failure (Enoiu et al., 2022), we expect that the SPICER assay will be able to resolve some unexplained cases of male infertility that result from loss of function of components of the fusion machinery.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enoiu et al., 2022.

claim: Other proteins essential for gamete fusion include SPACA6, TMEM95, TMEM81, FIMP, SOF1, and DCST1/2.
source: In this context, other proteins that are essential for gamete fusion, such as SPACA6, TMEM95, TMEM81, FIMP, SOF1, and DCST1/2 (Barbaux et al., 2020; Noda et al., 2020; Lorenzetti et al., 2014; Lamas-Toranzo et al., 2020; Fujihara et al., 2020; Inoue et al., 2021; Noda et al., 2022; Elofsson et al., 2023; Deneke et al., 2023), might be transferred to the somatic cells together with IZUMO1 during sperm-induced cell-cell fusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Barbaux et al., 2020; Noda et al., 2020; Lorenzetti et al., 2014; Lamas-Toranzo et al., 2020; Fujihara et al., 2020; Inoue et al., 2021; Noda et al., 2022; Elofsson et al., 2023; Deneke et al., 2023.

claim: Antibodies against IZUMO1 were detected on the sera of infertile women.
source: Finally, considering that antibodies against IZUMO1 were detected on the sera of infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013) and here, we observed that a monoclonal antibody against this protein was able to block sperm-induced syncytia, SPICER could serve as a tool to readily analyze cases of immuno-infertility.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clark and Naz, 2013.

claim: A monoclonal antibody against IZUMO1 was able to block sperm-induced syncytia.
source: Finally, considering that antibodies against IZUMO1 were detected on the sera of infertile women (Clark and Naz, 2013) and here, we observed that a monoclonal antibody against this protein was able to block sperm-induced syncytia, SPICER could serve as a tool to readily analyze cases of immuno-infertility.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The main caveat of the SPICER assay is that it cannot discriminate between defects in sperm docking or gamete fusion.
source: The main caveat of our assay is that it cannot discriminate between defects in sperm docking or gamete fusion, as a poor performance in SPICER could be explained by the altered interaction of IZUMO1 and JUNO or by a reduced capacity of IZUMO1 (and IZUMO1 partners in the sperm) to induce membrane merger.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors based on the mechanism of the assay.

claim: Simultaneous measurements of the levels of spontaneous acrosome reaction will be needed to exclude a faulty capacitation.
source: Moreover, simultaneous measurements of the levels of spontaneous acrosome reaction will be needed to exclude a faulty capacitation.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future implementation of the assay.

claim: Capacitation could be further stimulated pharmacologically using a Ca2+ ionophore.
source: Alternatively, capacitation could be further stimulated pharmacologically using a Ca2+ ionophore (Tateno et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tateno et al., 2013.

claim: Future validations using human sperm will be necessary for the establishment of an assay that could be used in the clinics.
source: As noted before, future validations using human sperm will be necessary for the establishment of an assay that could be used in the clinics.
evidence: This is a statement about future work needed for clinical application.
